title: Complete-reducibility criterion from splitting simple hyperplanes
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. A rational module for an affine finite-type $F$-group scheme $G$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism] means an $F$-vector space $V$ with a coaction $V\to V\otimes_F F[G]$ satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity. A submodule is a subspace whose coaction takes values in its tensor product with $F[G]$. A simple module is nonzero and has no proper nonzero submodule. An equivariant linear map means one commuting with coactions, equivalently with the actions after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. Suppose every character $G\to\mathbf G_m$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga], is the identity-valued group-scheme morphism. Assume that for every finite-dimensional rational module $U$ and every simple rational submodule $W\subseteq U$ with $\dim_F(U/W)=1$, there is a rational submodule $L\subseteq U$ with $U=W\oplus L$. Then every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module $V$ is a finite direct sum of simple rational submodules, allowing the empty sum for $V=0$.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text: Subspaces, inverse images and quotients used below carry their induced rational coactions: for a submodule $T\subseteq M$, set $\rho_{M/T}(m+T)=(q\otimes1)\rho_M(m)$, which is independent of the lift since $\rho_M(T)\subseteq T\otimes C$, where $C=F[G]$. The two coaction identities descend. Kernels of equivariant maps and inverse images of submodules are submodules: in bases adapted to a kernel, tensoring with the vector space $C$ preserves that kernel, so the coaction identity gives the assertion. These observations also apply to all scalar extensions; bases adapted to subspaces show exactness after extension.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text: First prove by strong induction on $n=\dim_F U$ that every rational submodule $W\subseteq U$ with $\dim(U/W)=1$ has a rational complement. There is no such pair for $n=0$. If $W=0$, take $U$ as complement. If $W$ is simple, use the hypothesis of the item. Otherwise choose a proper submodule $T\subsetneq W$ of maximal dimension. Because $W\ne0$ is not simple, such a $T$ can be chosen nonzero: the finite set of dimensions contains that of a proper nonzero submodule. The induced module $W/T$ is nonzero and simple, since the inverse image of any proper nonzero submodule would contradict maximality of $\dim T$.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text: The pair $W/T\subseteq U/T$ has simple hyperplane $W/T$, since the natural map $(U/T)/(W/T)\to U/W$ sends $(u+T)+(W/T)$ to $u+W$ and is a linear isomorphism. The assumed splitting therefore gives $U/T=(W/T)\oplus Q$, with $\dim Q=1$. Let $P\subseteq U$ be the inverse image of $Q$. Then $P/T=Q$, $P\cap W=T$, and $\dim P=\dim T+1<n$ (because $T\subsetneq W$). The induction hypothesis applied to the hyperplane $T\subseteq P$ gives $P=T\oplus L$ with $L$ rational and one-dimensional. Now $L\cap W\subseteq P\cap W=T$ and $L\cap T=0$, hence $L\cap W=0$; dimensions give $U=W\oplus L$. This closes the strong induction.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text: For an arbitrary finite-dimensional rational module $V$ and submodule $W$, the cases $W=0$ and $W=V$ have complements $V$ and $0$. Assume $0\ne W\ne V$. Apply [lem-sfb-rational-linear-hom] to obtain the finite-dimensional rational module $H=\operatorname{Hom}_F(V,W)$ with $(g\cdot f)(v)=g f(g^{-1}v)$ after every algebra extension. Applying the same node to $W,W$ gives the conjugation action on $E=\operatorname{End}_F(W)$. Restriction $r:H\to E$ is equivariant: for $w\in W_A$, $r(g\cdot f)(w)=g f(g^{-1}w)=(g\cdot r(f))(w)$.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text: The line $F\operatorname{id}_W\subseteq E$ is fixed under conjugation, because $g\operatorname{id}_{W_A}g^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_{W_A}$. Put $H_1=r^{-1}(F\operatorname{id}_W)$ and $H_0=\ker r$; these are rational submodules. Choose a basis of $W$, extend it to a basis of $V$, and define $p:V\to W$ to be the identity on the first basis and zero on the added vectors. Then $r(p)=\operatorname{id}_W\ne0$, so the map $H_1\to F$ sending $f$ to its unique scalar $a$ in $f|_W=a\operatorname{id}_W$ is surjective with kernel $H_0$. Thus $\dim(H_1/H_0)=1$. The hyperplane result just proved gives $H_1=H_0\oplus L$ with $L$ a one-dimensional rational submodule.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text: Choose $0\ne f\in L$. The action on the rational line $L$ defines a character $\chi:G\to\mathbf G_m$: in the basis $f$, write $g(f\otimes1)=\chi_A(g)(f\otimes1)$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$. These scalars are units because $g^{-1}$ acts inversely, are natural in $A$, and multiply under the group law. Equivalently the coaction is $f\mapsto f\otimes c$ with $c\in F[G]^\times$, $\Delta(c)=c\otimes c$ and $\epsilon(c)=1$, giving the coordinate morphism $F[t,t^{-1}]\to F[G]$, $t\mapsto c$. By the no-character hypothesis this character is trivial. Hence $f$ is fixed by the Hom action, and [lem-sfb-rational-linear-hom] implies that $f:V\to W$ is equivariant.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text:
Write $f|_W=a\operatorname{id}_W$. Since $L\cap H_0=0$ and $f\ne0$, we have $a\ne0$. Then $K=\ker f$ is a rational submodule. For each $v\in V$,
$$v=a^{-1}f(v)+(v-a^{-1}f(v)),$$
where the first summand lies in $W$ and the second in $K$, since $f$ acts by $a$ on $W$. If $w\in W\cap K$, then $0=f(w)=aw$, so $w=0$. Thus $V=W\oplus K$. We have proved that every rational submodule of every finite-dimensional rational module has a rational complement.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof.text: Finally induct on $\dim_F V$ to obtain the required finite simple decomposition. For $V=0$ use the empty sum. For $V\ne0$, choose a nonzero rational submodule $S$ of least positive dimension (the set of dimensions is nonempty because it contains $\dim V$). Every proper nonzero rational submodule of $S$ would have smaller dimension, so $S$ is simple. The complement property gives $V=S\oplus K$ with $\dim K<\dim V$. Decompose $K$ by induction and adjoin $S$. The submodules in that decomposition are rational submodules of $V$ by restriction of the coaction. This proves exactly the conclusion, including the zero-dimensional case.

source.place: Lemma 22.40, implication (c) to (a), printed pp.476-477; characteristic zero is the standing hypothesis on printed p.475.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 22.40 (c) to (b) to (a), printed pp.476-477; with the induction and zero cases written explicitly.
